Chapter 3: Deepening Focus and Building Intuition
As you gain experience, you’ll notice something changes. The basics just aren’t enough anymore. If you really want to grow, you’ve got to move past surface-level understanding and reach for true mastery.
It’s not just about knowing the rules—it's about absorbing them so deeply, they become second nature.
Picture this: you’re in a quiet practice room, staring at a single chess position. Instead of blitzing through dozens of puzzles, you laser in on just one. You’re not trying to memorize moves—you’re searching for the rhythms beneath the surface. The way pieces flow together, the push and pull of attack and defense, the tiny shifts in momentum. Hours might slip by, but you’re completely immersed, exploring every detail.
This technique—what some call making smaller circles—turns into a guiding principle. By drilling down into the fundamentals, you’re building a foundation sturdy enough to handle real pressure. So when the competition heats up, you don’t have to consciously think about every move. Your body and mind just respond, almost automatically, thanks to all those hours of focused practice.
And this mindset isn’t just for chess. Think about martial arts—a student might practice a single move over and over until it feels effortless. Or imagine a pianist, returning to a tricky passage, playing it slowly, then faster, then maybe even with their eyes closed. It can feel repetitive, even boring at times, but that’s the path to real breakthroughs. What used to feel stiff and awkward turns smooth. What used to take effort becomes pure instinct.
Here’s something most people miss: true mastery isn’t about doing more. It’s about doing less—just better. It’s stripping away the clutter, zeroing in on what matters most, and trusting that real depth will eventually give you real range. Suddenly, intuition doesn’t seem like magic anymore—it’s just the natural outcome of deep, focused work on the basics.
With practice, you’ll start to trust your instincts. In those high-pressure moments, there’s no panic—just a quiet confidence. Your mind stays clear, your body stays relaxed. Decisions come quickly, almost effortlessly. People might marvel at how easy it looks, but only you know the hours of deliberate practice that made it possible.
This slow, focused, intentional way of learning starts to shape everything you do. Whether you’re tackling something new or perfecting an old skill, you realize that real progress comes from going deep, not racing ahead. The journey never really ends—but now, the path feels a whole lot clearer.
